title: Knowledge and ignorance
note: Know the knowers: polymaths range across many fields, autodidacts teach themselves, dilettantes dabble, and neophytes have just begun. Empirical knowledge comes from observation; a priori knowledge comes from reasoning alone, before or apart from experience. Benighted once meant overtaken by night; now it means unenlightened.

read.title: What the Map Did Not Show
text: For centuries European mapmakers filled the unknown interior of Africa with elephants, rivers and invented kingdoms. The habit was not mere ignorance. A blank space looked like a failure, and a well-drawn guess passed easily for knowledge. Mapmakers copied one another, so a single conjecture could travel through a hundred atlases and acquire the look of empirical fact.

The most famous example was the Mountains of Kong, a range said to stretch across West Africa. It first appeared on a map in 1798, drawn from a traveler's report and a geographer's theory about where the Niger River must flow. No one had surveyed it, yet for nearly a century savants and atlas makers repeated it.

Between 1887 and 1889 the French explorer Louis-Gustave Binger traveled through the region and found no great mountain range at all. Mapmakers began to drop the range, slowly: one respected atlas still listed it in its index in 1928.

The lesson is not that early mapmakers were benighted. Many were astute scholars working with poor evidence. The trouble was that their maps were rarely cognizant of their own limits. A careful map, like a careful mind, marks the line between what is known and what is only supposed.

q.q: Why did the Mountains of Kong persist for so long?
o: They were visible from the coast
The mountains were higher than drawn
The Niger flowed through the range
There was no great mountain range
The maps had the right location

q.q: The passage says the maps were rarely "cognizant of their own limits," meaning they
o: did not show awareness of what was unknown
